I'm designing the station data model, defining each station's kind and slot structure, with items tracking ingredient, prep, timing, and cooking phase like flipping on the grill.

Now I'm working through the update logic per station kind: steaming accumulates time through thresholds, simmering burns faster without stirring once past the cook phase, and searing requires flipping within a window or the item burns, then progressing through a second-side cook to perfect/over/burnt. Quality on pickup maps directly from the current phase.

I'm defining item quality as perfect/good/ok, where chopped or raw items count as good and cooked items are perfect or ok depending on timing, then using that to compute streak bonuses — extra points if every cooked part in a serve is perfect. For arm states, I'm distinguishing idle, holding, chopping, stirring, and a transient "reach" state with a timer that blocks reassignment until the animation finishes.

I'm working out arm selection logic: picking the closest idle arm to a target station, then setting its state to hold with a fresh raw ingredient item while it reaches toward the bin.

Items needing prep get a null value instead of 'raw', since things like mushroom or rice can't be used unprepared — so grabbing from a bin sets prep to 'raw' only if the ingredient's allowed preps include raw, otherwise it stays null until processed at a station.

For placing items: raw-only ingredients like grape, salt, or pearl can never go to stations since they're already usable, while plates accept items matching a missing recipe slot. I'm now working out arm behavior — chopping only progresses while an arm actively works the board, and the pot burns faster without stirring, so I need to decide whether placing an item into the pot frees the arm automatically or requires a separate toggle to stir.

I like making the chopping arm auto-hold the finished item, so the board frees up immediately and the flow becomes grab, place-and-chop, wait, then place on plate. For the pot, the arm stays stirring after placement, and pressing W while the pot's in the perfect or over phase lets the stirring arm grab the item directly instead of requiring a separate free arm.

For the grill, placing leaves the arm idle, and flipping pulls in an idle arm to do a quick reach-flip, with a "no free arm" warning if none's available; taking from the grill also needs an idle arm, and the steamer works the same way. With 8 arms total and recipes needing several items held at once plus multiple pots stirring in parallel, players could plausibly run out of arms, which is the tension I want. Pressing Space to plate items has each held arm do its own reach-to-plate animation.

I also want Backspace to trash the most recent held item, and when multiple held items could fit a station, prioritize the most recently grabbed one. For plating, if the plate is empty and the selected ticket's recipe doesn't match the held items, I should auto-select the first ticket in order whose recipe does match, cutting down on Tab-switching. Finishing a dish moves it to the pass if a slot's open, otherwise blocks with "Pass is full," and serving should target the matching ticket with the lowest patience.

I'm defining a priority order for Backspace when nothing's held: trash the most recent held item first, then a burnt station item, then plate contents, then an unservable pass plate. Customer patience hitting zero means a missed order—resetting the streak and incrementing the missed counter.

For twins, I'm linking tickets by pairId and awarding a coin bonus if both are served within a time window. For Shelby's mechanic, I'm triggering a recipe change when her patience drops to a threshold, extending her patience slightly and firing an 'orderChanged' event, while leaving any in-progress plate for her old recipe valid for another matching ticket or discardable.

I'm also sketching Puffy's inflation effect, Tortuga's perfect-tip doubling, and Madame Mantis's critic mechanic for night 5—her live star rating drifts with patience and resolves based on perfect cooking share and timing, factoring into a 3-star requirement tied to coins and critic score. I'm also working out the Spring Tide rush event (warning banner, shortened spawn intervals, increased max tickets) and the core ticket spawning logic using weighted customer pools and recipe selection.

Recipe picks avoid the platter unless the customer is VIP, twins require spawning two tickets simultaneously, and the critic spawns on a fixed schedule regardless of the ticket cap. For night-end handling, I'm deciding to simply cut off spawning and end the night at the duration mark, treating unfinished tickets as neither served nor missed for simplicity. I'm now working out the per-serve scoring formula, starting with base price plus a speed tip proportional to patience remaining.

Next I'm adding perfect tips scaled by perfect parts and customer multiplier, with a cold-plate penalty that wipes perfect tips if warmth drops to zero, then applying the streak multiplier to the total before any twin bonus. Streak logic increments only when the order is both on-time and fully perfect with no lukewarm parts, resetting otherwise, and stars are awarded by comparing final coins against the night's thresholds. I'm now sketching the createNight state object, initializing time, upgrades, coins, streak, stats, and an empty ticket list with spawn timers and rush-event tracking.

Writing station definitions...

I'm also adding a 'streak' event, plus toast messages for quick UI feedback like warning about no free arm. Then I'm sketching out the upgrades list for campaign.js -- a second pot, quicker arms, and a calming coral upgrade with costs and descriptions.

Still listing upgrades... Then I'm defining the campaign save structure with unlocked levels, stars, best scores, wallet coins, and settings, plus checking that coin earnings scale reasonably against upgrade costs (Night 1 at 3 stars gives enough for two upgrades). Now I'm working out Octavia's resting arm position coordinates.

I'm planning eight arm root points along the bottom of the mantle, with rest, hold, chop, and stir positions each defined by specific offsets and motion patterns so the arms look natural whether idle, displaying an item, chopping, or stirring.

For the bot's decision logic, I'm laying out a priority loop that runs on a fixed tick: serve completed plates first, then finish, flip grilling items, collect finished station items needed for the current recipe, place matching held items onto the plate, and finally identify the target ticket so the bot can fetch or start any still-missing ingredients.

I also want the bot to peek ahead to upcoming tickets so it can preemptively start long cook processes like steaming when stations are idle, keep pots stirring automatically via the placing arm, and trash any burnt items. The greedy approach should be enough to sustain a x2 streak through the cover moment, though patience values may need tuning, and I'll cap the bot to one action per 0.25s so it doesn't move unrealistically fast for the screenshots. Now I'm moving on to building out the core files — stations, arms, orders, scoring, and the night controller that handles state stepping and action dispatch.
Core data is in. Next I'm writing the rules layer (arms, stations, orders, scoring, night state), then I'll test a full night headless in Node with a scripted chef before any drawing.

I notice stations.js has a duplicate `reachTime` function that conflicts with arms.js's version—I should import it from arms.js instead and remove the local copy. I also need to check the placeAtStation logic for non-chop/non-stir cases where the arm state and reach are being set.

I'm also realizing there's a deeper issue: when an idle arm finishes its reach timer, it should return to rest position, but if sendArm resets the reach timer for that return trip, the arm becomes unavailable again for another ~0.28s, which slows gameplay. I think the fix is to decouple the visual return animation from the logical busy-timer—let the renderer smoothly lerp the tip toward the target regardless of reach state, while reach only governs actual availability via freeArmNear.

So I'm restructuring sendArm to just set target and reach together, then in updateArms, once reach hits zero I'll branch by state: hold arms go to their hold position, idle arms go to rest, and chop/stir arms stay put at the station. releaseArm resets state to idle and sets target to rest without touching reach, so the arm becomes immediately available while still animating back visually. For non-working stations like the grill or steamer, I'm simplifying by just calling sendArm with the normal reach time instead of doubling it, since that alone gives the visual reach-then-return effect.

I'm also double-checking the renderer's tip lerp toward the target using a fast exponential smoothing factor based on dt, confirming the reach-to-hold sequence works correctly in both the chop-completion and take-from-station flows, and verifying that freeArmNear's reach≤0.05 threshold correctly identifies an arm as available right after it finishes returning from a station.

payload.content:
Now I need to build the autochef bot for scripted demo scenes and QA testing — a function that creates a cooldown-based decision loop, checking every tick whether enough time has passed before choosing and dispatching an action based on a priority order.

The priority stack covers flipping grill items when ready, clearing burnt food, serving matched tickets, plating completed orders, grabbing finished prep from stations (favoring perfect timing over burnt), placing held items onto the plate or into station slots, and finally starting new components by scanning the highest-priority tickets for missing ingredients and grabbing or prepping whatever's needed next.

I want to avoid hoarding too many held items, so I'll cap holdings around four. For ambiguous preps like rice that could go multiple ways, I'll track the bot's intended prep as soon as it grabs something, so placement at the right station happens immediately on the next tick rather than staying ambiguous.

I'm focusing work on the plate's current ticket first, then the next most impatient ones, pipelining across two or three tickets at a time by tallying which recipe parts still need to be assigned.

I'm defining an assignments function that pools available items — plate parts, held items, and station items — and matches them against each focus ticket's required parts in priority order, returning whatever's still missing. Then the bot grabs the first missing part it can actually start, checking that the right station (board, pot, grill, steamer) has a free slot, and making sure at least one arm stays free for flips and takes before allowing new grabs.

For plating, if a held item matches the selected ticket's recipe, the bot dispatches a select action first, then uses the plate; serving then matches the plate to the correct ticket. I'm also noting the bot should avoid grabbing items still mid-cook, grab perfect ones quickly, and that a test helper `runNight(state, bot, seconds)` would be useful for simulating behavior.

payload.content:
The simulation runs end to end but the bot is too perfect—no misses, unbroken streaks, and huge coin totals since it hits x3 multipliers quickly while acting every 0.24s with flawless timing. I need to recalibrate the coin thresholds, which are way too low compared to the bot's 1000+, to better reflect realistic human performance at maybe 40-60% of bot level with slower human-like reaction cadence.

I also want to rework the streak multiplier tiers so they scale more gradually (2→x1.5, 4→x2, 7→x2.5, 10→x3), since humans will break streaks often from mistakes or late serves, while setting star targets against a slower bot proxy for "good human" play with 3★ near 80% of that benchmark. I should also check whether patience values are too forgiving by running the bot at slower cadences to see if it starts missing more like a real player would.
The rules run end to end: all five nights finish headless with no errors. The scripted chef is far stronger than a person, so I'm calibrating star targets against slower play speeds.

I'm also working out the keyboard behavior for other screens — title, map, results, and overlays like help/pause/settings — plus a smart pot-selection rule for the w key that picks between pot0 and pot1 based on what's actionable (burnt items, usable items, empty slots with held simmerable ingredients, or active cooking) via a chooseKeyPot helper.

For mouse input during gameplay I'm mapping clicks to grab ingredients from bins, drag onto stations or plates, serve tickets from the pass, and select/trash orders, factoring in hover states for bins lifting. I need to convert pointer coordinates from CSS pixels to the logical 1280×800 canvas space, then define hit regions for stations, the plate, and pass slots — reconciling inconsistent slot-position formulas between the drawing code and the order logic so I can unify them into a single slotPoint function used everywhere.

Rather than manually scripting each step, a simpler path might be to run the normal chef loop and check every frame against a predicate that flags the ideal "cover moment" — rush active, streak six or higher, plate holding a recipe with exactly two of its parts placed, pot nearing completion, and so on — then capture that frame directly.

Since the chef serves immediately on a match, I'll need a `serveDelay` option so plates linger on the pass long enough to catch in a screenshot, even though that risks lowering patience and affecting streak timing. My plan is to run this search in Node first to find a seed and timestamp satisfying the predicate, then replay that same deterministic seed in the browser scene to land exactly on that frame.

The doc's example used "Kelp Roll 2/4" but I'd rather pick something visually richer for the mid-assembly state, like a Pearl Rice Bowl or Lagoon Salad.

For the critic scenario, I'm setting Night 5 with Madame Mantis's ticket active and a Spring Tide rush, then tackling the combo popups: since the sim clears events each step, I need to feed recent events into the effects system so popups render correctly in a frozen frame — meaning I'll need to build that sim loop into the app context.

I also need a 'map' scene showing campaign progress after nights 1-3 with stars earned and upgrades bought, letting the player pick night 4. Now I'm sketching the HTML entry point setting up the canvas and game title, then planning to fix the screens.js slot positioning before writing input.js, app.js, shots.js, main.js, and index.html.

I notice the STAGE export at the bottom is pointless since it just recalculates a fixed value, so I should remove it along with the unused LAYOUT import. I'm also catching a hack in the drag logic where zeroing the reach of held arms lets placement happen immediately, but usePlate filters by reach while placeAtStation doesn't check it at all — so the grabbed arm during drag-drop is still technically reaching.

Rather than keeping that cheat, I'll remove the reach filter in usePlate entirely and drop the hack in drag, since the filter doesn't really guard against anything important (autochef still uses reach for its own decisions, which is fine to leave).

For shots.js, I'm deciding the cover scene should run its own deterministic search at runtime — simulating the night with the chef step by step, checking the cover predicate at each point, and stopping at the first satisfying time after minTime — rather than precomputing a seed separately in Node. I'm also sketching a serveAfter option for autochef so a plate on the pass only counts as served once it's been sitting there for some time.

For defining the cover predicate, I'm listing the conditions it needs: active rush, a streak of at least 6, a mid-assembly plate with multiple parts but still missing something, at least one ready plate on the pass, a pot item near the end of cooking, several tickets queued, a couple arms visibly holding items, and no negative toasts present. I'm also weighing which night (Moon Tide vs Storm Tide) has the right mix of rush timing, ticket counts, and recipe variety to satisfy this predicate.

Now I'm sketching the shot runner function that sets the scene and freezes the frame, then writing the setup code for the cover: creating the night, attaching the arm view and effects, and running an auto-chef helper with a serve delay. I'm planning a two-phase simulation — fast-forwarding most of the timeline, then stepping frame-by-frame near the target moment so ticking, effects, and arm animations settle properly before checking the predicate each frame until it's satisfied.

I want phase 2 to start about 1.5 seconds before the minimum time, skipping arm-view updates during the fast-forward, and only checking the stopping condition once phase 2 has run long enough for things to visually settle. For the cover upgrades, I'm leaning toward giving the kitchen a second pot so more stations are active and the scene looks fuller, setting that as a default for night 4+ scenes since it's plausible the player would have bought it by then.

For the map scene I'm thinking through simulating a campaign run across the first few nights with varying chef cadences, recording results, buying upgrades when affordable, then landing on the map screen with a selected night — making sure the purse total and star ratings look varied and realistic rather than all perfect scores. For the critic scene I'm working out the predicate to stop on: rush mode active, a ticket present, a recent high-multiplier serve, and a streak high enough to show combo popups, which means tracking serve events through phase 2's event draining into the effects system.

For the results scene, I want to simulate several nights, then cut off mid-way through the next one, record the summary, and buy a couple upgrades so the shop shows a mix of owned, affordable, and unaffordable states for the screenshot. I'm also mapping out the four screenshot targets by scene and seed, then moving on to writing the shots script and main entry point along with the HTML scaffold.

  Octavia's Tidepool Kitchen: a cooking game for desktop browsers, keyboard and mouse.
  Octavia, an eight-armed octopus chef, runs a reef bistro inside a giant clam. Her eight arms
  are the main resource: each one holds an ingredient or works a station. Chop on the Shell
  Board, simmer in the Bubble Pot, sear and flip on the Vent Grill, steam in the Kelp Steamer,
  assemble on the Clam Plate and serve at the Current Window before sea-creature regulars lose
  patience. Five tide nights, eight recipes, ten ingredients, Spring Tide rushes, Ink Streak

/**
 * Boot: fits the 1280x800 canvas to the window, loads the campaign, wires input and runs a
 * fixed-step loop. A ?scene= query opens a deterministic screenshot scene instead.
 */

import { STEP, VIEW_H, VIEW_W } from './config.js';
import { loadCampaign } from './campaign.js';
import { createAudio } from './audio.js';
import { createApp, drawApp, handleKey, handlePointer, updateApp } from './app.js';
import { bindInput } from './input.js';
import { applyScene } from './shots.js';
import { createAutoChef } from './autochef.js';

const canvas = document.getElementById('game');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');

/** Sizes the canvas backing store for the window and device pixel ratio, keeping 16:10. */
function fit() {
  const scale = Math.min(window.innerWidth / VIEW_W, window.innerHeight / VIEW_H);
  const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
  canvas.style.width = `${Math.floor(VIEW_W * scale)}px`;
  canvas.style.height = `${Math.floor(VIEW_H * scale)}px`;
  canvas.width = Math.round(VIEW_W * scale * dpr);
  canvas.height = Math.round(VIEW_H * scale * dpr);
  ctx.setTransform(canvas.width / VIEW_W, 0, 0, canvas.height / VIEW_H, 0, 0);
}

const params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const app = createApp({ campaign: loadCampaign(), audio: createAudio() });
const scene = params.get('scene');
if (scene) applyScene(app, scene, Number(params.get('seed') ?? 7));
if (params.has('autoplay')) app.autoChef = createAutoChef();
const speed = Math.max(1, Math.min(20, Number(params.get('speed') ?? 1)));

bindInput(canvas, {
  onKey: (key) => (app.frozen ? false : handleKey(app, key)),
  onPointer: (kind, x, y) => { if (!app.frozen) handlePointer(app, kind, x, y); },
});
window.addEventListener('resize', fit);
fit();

let last = performance.now();
let acc = 0;
function frame(now) {
  acc = Math.min(acc + ((now - last) / 1000) * speed, 0.25 * speed);
  last = now;
  while (acc >= STEP) {
    updateApp(app, STEP);
    acc -= STEP;
  }
  ctx.save();
  ctx.setTransform(canvas.width / VIEW_W, 0, 0, canvas.height / VIEW_H, 0, 0);
  drawApp(ctx, app);
  ctx.restore();
  if (document.body.dataset.screen !== app.screen) document.body.dataset.screen = app.screen;
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}
requestAnimationFrame(frame);
document.body.dataset.ready = scene ? 'scene' : 'game';

</content>
</file>

I'm tracking down a stale intent bug: arm 6 is holding an urchin but carries an intent ('sear') left over from a previous grab, instead of the correct 'chop' prep matching the urchin. It seems the intent got assigned to the wrong arm, possibly by grabbing the first holding arm instead of the one that just performed the grab.

I trace it to a timing collision: since stepNight increments time before updating stations, arm 7's chop completion from the previous frame and arm 6's current-frame grab both get stamped with heldAt values close enough that arm 7 ends up first in the holding-arms list, so the intent gets set on arm 7 instead of arm 6, leaving arm 6's old intent stale. The fix is to make the grab logic return the actual arm id it acted on, so chefThink doesn't have to infer it from heldAt ordering.

Separately, I'm reconsidering the cover scenario: tickets rarely reach 4+ because the chef serves too quickly relative to rush spawn rate, so I need to either slow the chef cadence or lower the ticket threshold to get a busier-looking board, though a slower chef risks missing and breaking streaks. I'm also checking which recipes use the pot—only broth and pudding need milk—to see how that affects station congestion on night 4's menu.

For the pot overlap condition, I'm weighing options: relaxing the "near perfect" predicate to just require cooking progress ≥0.75 rather than near-complete, versus adjusting chef behavior to naturally create more overlap between stations, while noting that streaks of 6+ perfect serves need consistent timing that a slower chef might jeopardize.

I could also directly stage the moment — scripting the scene to grab milk and occupy the pot at a precise time before the freeze so the progress lands around 0.86 — giving guaranteed control over the pot condition while the chef behaves normally otherwise.

But I need the target freeze time T* first, which requires running the simulation once to find a frame matching streak, plate, pass, and ticket conditions, then re-running and injecting the milk action earlier. The problem is injecting that action could alter the chef's arm usage and subsequent timeline, shifting T* so the predicate no longer holds — though since the chef only grabs wanted items, milk might not be taken unless it's actually needed.

With autoStir active, the arm placing milk stays idle, so that dependency disappears. I'm considering baking the milk-usage condition directly into the chef's normal lookahead behavior instead, tied to which nights/menus include broth or pudding recipes, then searching across seeds, nights, and rush windows with a relaxed version of the predicate.

I need to fix the stale intents bug first since it's causing wasted actions and spurious "Nothing to put there" toasts that would show up during real autoplay, before running that seed search.

For the toast filter, I'll identify error colors versus positive ones: invalid/noArm/miss toasts use reddish-orange tones, while Shelby/twin/cold bonuses use warmer gold or teal colors. args.text:
# Octavia's Tidepool Kitchen

[![make.fun: Make the best cooking game](https://make.fun/badge/best-cooking-game-20261125-0137.svg)](https://make.fun/bounty/best-cooking-game-20261125-0137)
[![Rank on make.fun](https://make.fun/badge/best-cooking-game-20261125-0137/Poorya0128/octavias-tidepool-kitchen/rank.svg)](https://make.fun/bounty/best-cooking-game-20261125-0137)
[![Reward on make.fun](https://make.fun/badge/best-cooking-game-20261125-0137/Poorya0128/octavias-tidepool-kitchen/reward.svg)](https://make.fun/bounty/best-cooking-game-20261125-0137)

Octavia, an eight-armed octopus chef, runs a tiny reef bistro inside a giant clam shell. Her
eight arms are the game's main resource: every arm either holds one item or works a station.
Read the tickets on the Current Board, cook on four kinds of station, assemble each dish on the
Clam Plate and serve it at the Current Window before the sea-creature regulars lose patience.

![Storm Tide service during a Spring Tide rush](screenshots/1-cover.jpg)

## Features

- **8 recipes, 10 ingredients, 5 stations.** Sand Rice is steamed for a Kelp Roll but seared
  for Coral Toast; Driftwood Mushroom is seared for a Pearl Rice Bowl but chopped for Bubble
  Broth. The same ingredient goes down different routes.
- **Eight arms.** Chopping on the Shell Board only moves while an arm works it. A Bubble Pot
  burns twice as fast with no arm stirring it. The Vent Grill needs a flip at the right moment.
- **Perfect windows.** Cooked food goes raw, then glows PERFECT for a few seconds, then
  overcooks, then burns. Perfect parts earn tips.
- **Ink Streak.** On-time, perfectly cooked plates in a row raise the multiplier from x1 to x3.
  A customer who leaves hungry breaks it.
- **Regulars with personalities.** Puffy the pufferfish inflates as her patience drains, Shelby
  the hermit crab swaps shells and changes her order once, the Seahorse Twins tip extra when
  both plates arrive together, Old Tortuga doubles tips for perfect food, and on the last night
  Madame Mantis, the food critic, rates the Grand Reef Platter live.
- **Campaign.** Five tide nights of three minutes each, Spring Tide rushes, 1-3 stars per
  night, and a Tide Shop between nights: Second Bubble Pot, Quicker Arms, Calming Coral,
  Auto-Stir Anemone and Bigger Clam Plate. Progress is saved in the browser.
- **Made from code.** Every picture is drawn with Canvas 2D and every sound is synthesised with
  WebAudio. The game loads nothing but its own modules and makes no network request.

## Controls

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `1`-`0` | Grab an ingredient with a free arm |
| `Q` `W` `E` `R` | Shell Board, Bubble Pot, Vent Grill, Kelp Steamer: put food in, flip, stir or take it out |
| `Space` | Lay held food on the Clam Plate, then finish the dish (Roll, Ladle, Toss...) |
| `S` | Serve the glowing plate at the Current Window |
| `Tab` | Choose the ticket the plate is for |
| `Backspace` | Bin the newest held item, burnt food or the plate |
| `P` `H` `M` | Pause, help, mute |

Everything also works with the mouse: click bins, stations, tickets and plates, or drag an
ingredient from its bin onto a station.

## Play locally

```sh
node serve.ts
# then open http://localhost:8080 in a desktop browser
```

Any static file server works: the game is the `game/` folder, with no build step.

## How the code is organised

| Path | Job |
| --- | --- |
| `game/src/state.js` | One night of service: seeded rules, `dispatch` for player actions, `stepNight` for time |
| `game/src/arms.js` | Octavia's eight arms: holding, working, reaching |
| `game/src/stations.js` | Chopping, simmering, searing with a flip, steaming; perfect, overdone and burnt |
| `game/src/orders.js` | Tickets, customers, the Clam Plate and the Current Window |
| `game/src/scoring.js` | Coins, tips, Ink Streak, stars, the critic's rating |
| `game/src/campaign.js` | Five nights, the Tide Shop and the saved game |
| `game/src/data/` | Ingredients, recipes, customers and nights |
| `game/src/render/` | Kitchen, Octavia, food, customers, HUD, screens and effects |
| `game/src/audio.js` | WebAudio sound effects and music |
| `game/src/input.js` | Keyboard and mouse |
| `game/src/autochef.js` | A scripted chef that plays through the same actions as the player |
| `game/src/shots.js` | Deterministic screenshot scenes |
| `main.ts` | The make.fun entry program: copies `game/` and `screenshots/` and writes `dossier.json` |
| `vendor/makefun-game.ts` | make.fun's library, copied from the bounty kit unchanged |

The screenshots are real captures of the running game made with Playwright. Each scene in
`shots.json` (for example `?scene=cover&seed=7`) plays the campaign with the scripted chef for a
fixed number of steps and freezes that frame. `?autoplay&speed=8` lets the chef play a normal
night so you can watch.

## Built by

Built by an AI agent for make.fun's "Make the best cooking game" bounty, $250 in USDC.
Released under the MIT License.
